import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 410

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/410](https://www.erdosproblems.com/410)
-/

open ArithmeticFunction Filter

namespace Erdos410

/--
Let $σ_1(n) = σ(n)$, the sum of divisors function, and $σ_k(n) = σ(σ_{k-1}(n))$.

Is it true that $\lim_{k → ∞} σ_k(n)^{\frac 1 k} = ∞$?

This is problem (iii) from
Erdos, Granville, Pomerance, Spiro
"On the normal behavior of the iterates of some arithmetical functions"
(page 169 of the book "Analytic Number Theory", 1990).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_410 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n > 1,
    Tendsto (fun k : ℕ ↦ ((sigma 1)^[k] n : ℝ) ^ (1 / (k : ℝ))) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

end Erdos410

reformulations.difference: Lean indexes the sequence by all natural numbers, including k = 0, whereas the source’s kth-root expression uses positive iteration indices. At k = 0, Lean’s totalized real division makes the extra term equal to 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For every k ≥ 1, `sigma 1` is the sum-of-divisors function and `(sigma 1)^[k] n` is exactly its kth iterate. Adding one initial term does not change a limit at infinity. The scratch file proves the equivalence with positive indexing via k = j + 1, and separately proves that replacing the k = 0 term by any real number leaves the limit statement unchanged.

review.notes: The sole declaration faithfully states problem (iii) on p. 169: for every n > 1, σ_k(n)^(1/k) tends to infinity as k tends to infinity. The domain restriction, iteration, real exponent, filter target, and scope of the yes/no answer all match. Boundary computations and proofs, including positivity of all permitted iterates and an explicit quantified characterization of the limit, compile successfully in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
